To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
D‐cycloserin (DCS)‐augmented one-session treatment (OST) is effective in treating specific phobias (SPs) in children and adolescents, and that DCS is more effective for children than adolescents.
DCS‐augmentation did not improve OST outcomes for specific phobia in children, and that DCS‐enhanced OST may be more effective in adolescents.
D‐cycloserines effects are not consistent across studies and that the results are not clear enough to recommend its use.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the treatment and prevention of specific childhood phobias.
the effects of DCS augmentation of one‐session exposure therapy in youth with phobias.
the effects of DCS‐OST on youth phobia and with identifying moderators of treatment outcome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DCS augmentation to OST for specific phobia in youth is promising but needs to be replicated in a larger sample with longer follow‐up periods.
D‐cycloserines augmentation of one‐session treatment for specific phobia is not recommended.
DCS did not appear to be associated with greater benefits than placebo in youth with specific phobia, but that there was a trend towards a greater benefit for DCS among children than adolescents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
D‐cycloserines effects on treatment outcome are likely dependent on the specific phobia, age, and fear level of participants, which should be considered when planning future trials of D‐cycloserine.
D‐cycloseride‐augmented one session exposure therapy for specific phobia is a safe and promising intervention.
DCS‐augmentation of OST for youth with specific phobias was safe and well‐tolerated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
D‐cycloserie may be a useful adjunct to one‐session exposure therapy for children and adolescents with specific phobias.
D‐cyclosering is not a panacea for all phobic conditions, nor for all patients, and that it is important to consider the patient’s age, the type of fear, and the type of treatment.
